entry.title: Week 7: Where I've actually got to
entry.content:
Week 7 · 16 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Seven weeks in — this session is a checkpoint: reviewing where I am in the course and planning the next stretch.

1. What I worked on

Building this website and mapping out my progress: which sessions happened, what I covered in each, and what’s still ahead in Chapter 1.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The main challenge this week was stepping back from the course content to take stock of the bigger picture. It’s easy to stay heads-down watching the next video, but a checkpoint like this forces me to ask whether the pace makes sense and whether I’m actually retaining what I’ve learned.

Setting up the site itself took some decisions — choosing Hexo with the Fluid theme, organising the journal entries by week, adding a resources page with all the course links. I wanted the site to be functional and easy to maintain rather than flashy, since the point is the learning journal, not the web design.

Looking at the five sessions so far, I can see a clear progression through Chapter 1 (绪论): from choosing the course, to understanding what computation means, to learning how to measure algorithms, to the Turing machine model. Each session built on the previous one, and the pace has been steady — about two or three lecture videos per session plus exercises.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I’ve been consistent across all five sessions — showing up prepared, engaging with the material, and building understanding incrementally. The course choice in week 1 was mine, and I’ve maintained focus through conceptual material that doesn’t always have immediate practical payoff. This checkpoint itself is an example of managing my learning: reviewing progress and planning ahead rather than just continuing on autopilot. Not 100 because I could be doing more outside of class time — reviewing between sessions, trying additional problems, or exploring topics beyond what the videos cover.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Start submitting to the online judge. The next topics — the RAM model and big-O notation — should give me opportunities to write and test actual code. I also want to establish a routine of reviewing notes between sessions so each Friday starts with context instead of a cold start.

entry.title: Week 5: Turing machines
entry.content:
Week 5 · 2 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Back after a two-week gap — last Friday was Mid-Autumn Festival, so no class on the 25th.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B2: the Turing machine model and a worked example of one running. Two videos plus tracing through the example on paper.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The Turing machine components — tape, read/write head, alphabet, state set, transition function — are straightforward individually, but keeping track of all of them at once while tracing an execution took practice. A transition rule like (q, c) → (p, d, L/R) means “if you’re in state q reading character c, write d, move left or right, and switch to state p.” I found that writing it out in words like this helped me internalise it.

When I traced B2-2’s example on paper, I initially read the transition table top-to-bottom like code. Once I switched to treating it as a lookup table — find your current (state, character) pair, read off what to do — everything clicked and I could trace the whole execution smoothly. That shift in how I was reading the table was the key insight of this session.

The bigger conceptual question is why Turing machines matter when nobody builds them. By the end of the second video I could see the point: it’s about defining what “computable” means, so later the course can talk about whether a problem is solvable at all, not just how fast. It connects computation theory to the practical algorithm work coming up.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I engaged well with the material — traced the example on paper rather than just watching, caught my own misreading of the transition table and corrected it, and pushed through the more abstract parts until I understood why they matter. I also spent the first few minutes reviewing my notes from week 3 to reconnect with where I’d left off, which helped me get into the session faster. Not 100 because I stayed within the course material rather than exploring related ideas on my own.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Before class, spend ten minutes reviewing the previous session’s notes. The two-week gap made it clear that a quick review at the start saves time overall. Also, I want to look ahead at what’s next — B3 on the RAM model and then big-O notation — so I have context for where these concepts are leading.

Evidence

Paper trace of the B2-2 Turing machine example. No OJ submissions — the Turing machine section is conceptual with written exercises.

entry.title: Week 3: How you measure an algorithm
entry.content:
Week 3 · 18 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

All theory this week — how to measure how good an algorithm is without actually running it.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B1: performance measurement, problem size, worst-case analysis, and the idealised computation model. Four videos and the associated exercises.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The first concept that took real thought was why you can’t just time your code. I knew from competitive programming that the same code runs differently on different machines, but I hadn’t framed it formally before. The answer is you count operations instead of seconds, which removes the hardware from the equation — and then you need to define what counts as an “operation,” which is where the idealised model comes in.

Writing cost as T(n) instead of a single number took a moment to get used to. For sorting, n is the number of elements; for multiplying two numbers, n is the number of digits. They’re both called n but they measure completely different things, and the function T means something different in each case. I paused the video and worked through this with my own examples until it felt natural.

Worst-case analysis I actually found intuitive — in competitive programming you always think about the worst input because that’s what gets you TLE. What the course added was framing this as a deliberate choice: you could analyse the average case instead, and sometimes that’s more useful, but worst-case is the default because it gives a guarantee. Seeing it presented as a modelling decision connected the formal theory to the practical intuition I already had, which was satisfying.

The idealised model that abstracts away cache, word length, and memory speed made me think about when simplifications are useful versus when they hide something important. The course’s argument — that you need to abstract to say anything general — is convincing, and I can see how it connects to big-O notation coming up next.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

This was my most focused session so far. The content is conceptual with no code to write, which can be harder to stay engaged with, but I kept finding connections to things I already knew from competitive programming. The gap between “sort of knowing” and formally understanding was bigger than I expected, and closing that gap felt productive. Not 100 because I followed the planned sequence without looking ahead or generating my own examples beyond what the exercises asked for.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

After each video, close the tab and restate the main idea in one sentence before moving on. This helps me check whether I actually understood it or just followed along.

Evidence

Notes on T(n), worst-case vs average-case, and the idealised model. No OJ submissions — this section of the course is all conceptual with written exercises.

entry.title: Week 2: Setting up, and what “computation” means
entry.content:
Week 2 · 11 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

First real session with the course material — got everything set up and started the opening lectures.

1. What I worked on

Enrolled on XuetangX, registered on the Tsinghua online judge with the same email, and got g++ working locally with -std=c++14. Then watched 绪论 A — the videos on what “computation” actually means.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The lecture content was unexpected. I came in expecting code and got rope computers and straightedge constructions. At first I wasn’t sure where it was going, but by the end of the video I got the point: these are examples of “basic operations” in different computational models, and the whole idea of analysing algorithms depends on agreeing what counts as one step. It clicked when he showed that a straightedge can do addition — I’d never thought of geometry that way before.

The four properties of an algorithm — correctness, determinism, feasibility, finiteness — took some effort to keep straight. Feasibility means each step is actually doable; finiteness means it terminates. The Hailstone sequence was the example that made this stick: it’s a perfectly valid program, every step is simple, but nobody can prove it always terminates, so it’s not an algorithm. It’s interesting that such a simple program is still an open problem in mathematics.

I also figured out the OJ registration — the account email has to match the XuetangX one for grades to sync. Caught that early by reading the instructions carefully.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I got through everything I planned and made a real effort to understand the concepts rather than just watching passively. I paused videos to think through the examples and made sure I could explain each of the four algorithm properties before moving on. Not 100 because I stuck to the planned material without exploring anything beyond it.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Front-load any admin or setup tasks so the full period goes to course content. 45 minutes is enough for two or three videos plus exercises if I use it well.

Evidence

Registered on XuetangX and the OJ. Notes from 绪论 A on the four algorithm properties and the Hailstone example.

entry.title: Week 1: Picking the course took longer than I thought it would
entry.content:
Week 1 · 4 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

This session was deciding what my VLD actually is. The direction was clear — data structures and algorithms, in C++ — but choosing the right course turned out to be a real decision.

1. What I worked on

Comparing four candidate courses and committing to one: Tsinghua University’s Data Structures (数据结构), taught by Prof. Deng Junhui, free on XuetangX. I also read through the prerequisites and found the online judge where programming assignments get submitted.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The hard part was that every obvious option had a catch, and I couldn’t tell which one mattered until I worked out what I actually needed.

  • Stanford CS106B — everything’s public and it’s in C++, but nothing I submit gets marked.
  • UC San Diego’s specialisation on Coursera — properly graded, but it needs a financial-aid application, and it mixes Python, Java and C++.
  • UIUC Accelerated CS Fundamentals — C++, free to audit, closest to a drop-in answer. But about 60 hours total, which is thin for a whole year.
  • Tsinghua’s 数据结构 — free, entirely C++, and it has a real online judge with graded assignments.

I wrote down the three things I actually needed — work that gets graded, C++ throughout, and no cost — and only one option had all three. That’s how I got unstuck: the comparison was impossible until I’d decided what I was comparing on.

I also considered skipping a formal course and just grinding problems on USACO Guide and CSES, since I have a competitive programming background. But I decided against it: problem sets teach you to recognise patterns you’ve already seen, while a structured course builds the foundations I want to strengthen — things like templates, virtual methods, and formal algorithm analysis.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I made a real decision and I can defend it. I set my own criteria, evaluated four options against them, and committed to one with a clear rationale. The reason it’s 89 and not 100 is that listing the criteria should have been my starting point instead of something I arrived at after browsing course pages for a while — once I had the criteria, the decision was fast.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Send Mr. Wright the course link and my one-sentence reason before I do anything else, then enrol and register on the judge in the same session — registration needs to use the same email as the XuetangX account or the grades don’t sync.
